transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Stocks opened higher this morning as crude oil prices fall.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones industrial average jumped more than 560 points
in early trading.
Crude oil prices dropped sharply on hopes for a diplomatic push to ease the standoff between
the U.S. and Iran, which is royal energy markets.
The U.S. benchmark for crude oil fell below $100 a barrel after news that Iranian negotiators
were in Qatar for talks over the weekend.
Retail gasoline and diesel prices both dipped by about a penny a gallon overnight.
There may also be a thaw in the U.S. trade war with next-door neighbor Canada.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he's had a productive conversation with President
Trump.
Talks had stalled over the summer, leading to more tariffs.
And Apple is set to report quarterly earnings after the market closes this afternoon.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
There is still surprise over Michigan Democratic Congresswoman Hailey Stevens' decision to
pull her endorsement of Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
Stevens lost the Democratic Senate primary to El-Sayed earlier this year.
Yesterday, Stevens suddenly endorsed Republican Mike Rogers, after repeatedly telling other
Democrats she would back El-Sayed.
She defended her decision to CNN's Anderson Cooper.
"I am not trying to upset anyone, I'm just being honest with my constituents and what
I'm hearing from people.
And in fact, I've been hearing from a ton of dems Anderson who said, 'Thank you.
This is how we felt.
We haven't liked this campaign.
It's painful.'"
There has been discord between Hailey Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed.
Yesterday, El-Sayed said he would remain focused on the needs of Michigan voters.
"My focus has never wavered.
I have been clear about what our responsibilities are.
So rather than focus on a distraction about who said what to whom, where they went, I've
been consistent.
I want to get money out of politics.
I want to put money back in pockets."
He was heard here on CNN.
The Trump administration is asking a federal appeals court to revive its push to block
the results of Alaska's Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses.
And PR's Hansi Lo Wang reports a lower court said the administration doesn't have the
ability to challenge this.
The Trump administration is asking federal courts to stop Alaska from certifying its
U.S. Senate race results to allow for an investigation into whether voters were confused by having
two candidates with similar names on the ballot.
But U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason found that would likely violate voters' right to
keep whom they voted for a secret.
And Trump said he ordered this lawsuit to be filed because of allegations that Democrats
propped up Daniel Sullivan Jr. as a candidate to spoil the chances of Republican Senator
Dan Sullivan of winning reelection.
The Justice Department and the state of Alaska have started investigations.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
It's NPR.
There are fresh evacuation notices in northern New Mexico.
The San Juan River is flooding and authorities are telling people to get to higher ground.
Officials in southern Colorado are also telling some people to flee.
The same weather system swept through central Arizona earlier.
From member station KNAU and Flagstaff, Chris Clements reports.
Oak Creek near Sedona typically flows at a trickle this time of year.
This weekend it was a churning, torrential Brown River.
After it jumped its banks, it trapped residents in Sedona, leading to rooftop evacuations and
damaged property.
Jenny Kittridge manages a hotel along Oak Creek and says while her property hasn't been
damaged yet as of Sunday afternoon, the creek was just below the deck of her lowest structure.
It was, yeah, the highest I've ever seen it in my 33 years here.
The downpour brought a fresh round of flooding to tribal communities like the Navajo and
Hopi reservations and caused the Verde and Salt Rivers to rise.
For NPR News, I'm Chris Clements in Flagstaff.
Enrolment is now open for the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.
That includes healthcare.gov.
These are for people who do not get health insurance through their jobs or don't qualify
for public programs.
The Trump administration says fewer people are now enrolled because they were ineligible
or were "fantom."
Health experts say it is more likely that millions of people are not enrolling because
they cannot afford the premiums anymore.
And lawmakers declined to extend extra money to keep premiums at a lower cost.
This is NPR.
This message comes from Rosetta Stone.
Rosetta Stone is designed to make language learning intuitive.
It mimics how people naturally acquire speech as children, helping users read, write, and
think in a second language.
More at RosettaStone.com.

topics.text: Stocks open higher as crude oil falls on hopes of U.S.-Iran diplomatic talks in Qatar
Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney have a productive call, signaling possible easing of trade tensions
Apple set to report quarterly earnings after the market closes this afternoon
Rep. Hailey Stevens pulls endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed and backs Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan Senate race
Trump administration asks appeals court to revive bid to block Alaska Senate race certification over ballot confusion
Flash flooding prompts new evacuation notices in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado
Oak Creek floods Sedona, Arizona, forcing rooftop evacuations and damaging property
Enrollment opens for Affordable Care Act marketplaces as fewer people sign up amid premium costs
